To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the "first hit" in the development of alcoholism involves brain-generated EtOH acetaldehyde and/or salsolinol that act on specific brain areas and that the "second hit" involves other brain systems.

the brain metabolites acetaldehyde, salsolinol, and acetate are reinforcing at low concentrations, and that these brain-generated metabolites are involved in the early ("the first-hit") development of EtOH reinforcement.
the brain-generated EtOH metabolic products acetaldehyde and/or salsolinol are self-administerable into the brain and are reinforcing.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the neurochemical and behavioral mechanisms that underlie the development of alcohol reinforcement in humans and animals.
the identification of the neurobiological mechanisms underlying the reinforcing and relapse-inducing effects of EtOH, and the identification of potential targets for novel pharmacotherapies.
the development of a model that explains the "first-hit" toward EtOH reinforcement, the "second-hit" toward alcoholism, and the maintenance of the "third hit" toward relapse.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
EtOH metabolites are the "first-hit" toward EtOH reinforcement.
brain-generated EtHO metabolites are the "first hit" that leads to alcohol addiction.
brain-generated EtOh metabolites are the first "hits" that initiate alcohol reinforcement and relapse.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
EtOH is a drug that is consumed to attain milligram per kilogram concentrations in the blood and brain.
the brain-generated EtOH-metabolites, acetaldehyde and, to a lesser degree, salsolinol, are major contributors to the development of alcohol reinforcement.
the "first-hit" toward alcohol reinforcement is the brain-generated EtOH, but that the "second-hit" is a metabolite of EtOH.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the "first hit" of EtOH generates a cascade of brain events that leads to alcohol addiction.
the brain is the major site of alcohol's action, and it is the brain that is responsible for alcohol's reinforcing and relapse-like properties.
EtOH is not a single entity, but is a mixture of several pharmacologically active compounds, some of which are generated in the brain and others in the liver.
